games.summary:
The session's web-search budget had run out (200 of 200), so I worked from pages I could fetch directly, mostly Wikipedia in several languages, plus GamesRadar, the CK3 wiki and Steam. Figures marked "estimate" or "my calc" are my own or general knowledge, not published numbers. No firm published figures turned up for the size of Black Flag's or Sea of Thieves' map, for Naval Action or World of Sea Battle, or for the scale of Ghost of Tsushima.

Main result: the closest model to Kapman is Euro Truck Simulator 2. Its trucks drive at real speed through a 1:19 world. Its clock runs at about 20x, so speeds read true on the clock. Its cities are drawn much bigger than the land between them (the clock runs 3x in cities, so cities are roughly 1:3).

The AAA games compress about as much as Kapman does: AC Odyssey is about 1:38 (estimate) and The Crew about 1:45 (my calc). But their horses, cars and warships are 5-15x faster than a 2.25 m/s boat, so the same scale gives Kapman much longer trips.

Kapman's clock is 60x, so 1:60 is the scale where the boat reads its true speed by the game clock. At 1:40 it reads 1.5 m/s (2.9 kn), and every voyage takes 1.5x the real number of days.

Real-time Dorestad to London (about 430 km) by scale, for the comparison maps:
- 1:1 — about 53 h
- 1:20 — about 2.7 h
- 1:32 — about 1.7 h
- 1:40 — about 1.3-1.6 h
- 1:60 — about 53 min
- 1:100 — about 32 min

What works across these games:
1. **Uneven scale.** Towns, harbours, river mouths and rivers are drawn big (1:1 to 1:3); the open sea is shrunk the most.
2. **Something every 10-30 minutes.** Sea of Thieves aimed for another ship every 15-30 minutes. There should also be work on board.
3. **Familiar outlines.** Coastlines stay recognisable, while the land inside is reshaped for play.
4. **Fewer towns at smaller scales.** Valhalla shows 3 walled cities for all of England.
5. **The 2D chart counts days and supplies.** Long voyages feel long through days passing, supplies and events triggered by distance, not through real minutes.

findings.name: Euro Truck Simulator 2 / American Truck Simulator (the closest model)
findings.what: Trucks drive at real speed across a shrunk Europe or USA. The game clock speeds up to match the shrink, and cities are drawn much bigger than the countryside: the clock runs slower in cities, so cities are effectively less shrunk.
findings.numbers: ETS2: Europe at 1:19, the UK at 1:15 (an older build SCS says it will fix in a UK rework). ATS: the USA at 1:20. Clock: 1 game minute = 3 real seconds outside towns (20x) and 20 real seconds in cities (3x), which means cities are about 1:3 (my inference). With a 20x clock on a 1:19 map, an 80 km/h truck reads about 76 km/h by the clock, so speeds look honest. A long 1,000-2,000 real-km job takes about 40-80 real minutes (my calc). Base game: 71 cities in 12 countries. Liked: map size and road variety ('unexpectedly engrossing'). Disliked: cities as 'the shortest of visual shorthand - a few warehouses, the odd landmark', and no hedgerows.
findings.lesson: Match the clock to the scale. Kapman's 60x clock on a 1:40 map makes the boat read 1.5 m/s (2.9 kn) by the game clock, so every voyage takes 1.5x the period's real days. At 1:60 the boat reads its true 2.25 m/s, the same honesty ETS2 has. Uneven scale (towns several times larger than the land between) is accepted by players; complaints start only when towns become too sketchy.

findings.name: The Crew (whole USA, condensed)
findings.what: The whole continental USA is driveable, built around a handful of big cities, with geography bent to make them fit.
findings.numbers: The map is 'about 2000 times smaller' than the real USA. That must be area (a 1:2000 length scale would make the country 2 km wide), so the length scale is about 1:45 (my conversion). Coast to coast takes about 45 real minutes. Five regions; 6 main cities (Detroit, Chicago, NYC, Miami, Las Vegas, LA) plus about 9 smaller ones (St Louis, DC, New Orleans, Seattle and others). The article says it 'contains geographical inaccuracies to fit the cities and landmarks into the scale'.
findings.lesson: About 1:45 works for a continent at car speed (30+ m/s). A 2.25 m/s boat is roughly 15x slower, so the same shrink gives roughly 15x longer trips: a 4,500 km crossing at 1:45 would take about 12 real hours by boat (my calc). Small towns are cut and the big ones are kept and moved slightly to fit, which is what the user proposed for the smaller-scale maps.

findings.name: Assassin's Creed Odyssey (Greece and the Aegean)
findings.what: Mainland Greece and the Aegean islands, sailed in the warship Adrestia, with fast-travel points.
findings.numbers: The map is 16 x 16 km = 256 km². The real area it covers (Kephallonia to Lesbos, Makedonia to Crete) is about 600 x 620 km (estimate), so the length scale is about 1:38 (estimate), almost Kapman's 1:40. The developers stripped trees off mountain peaks and added fog so the shrunk mountains would read as big. Reception: the world was praised, but the game was called 'too repetitive and bloated with content'.
findings.lesson: At about 1:40 the Aegean still read as Greece, but with a much faster ship and fast travel. Cheap tricks that sell size, such as haze, distance fog and bare peaks, carry over directly to a 1:40-1:60 sea. Bloat came from filler content, not from distance.

findings.name: Assassin's Creed Valhalla (England, Norway, river longship)
findings.what: England is 'not quite to scale' and split into counties. Norway is a smaller separate map. The longship is mostly river transport for raids. Later updates added River Raids: separate replayable river maps of parts of England not on the main map.
findings.numbers: England has 13 counties, 3 regions (Northumbria, Mercia, Wessex) and only 3 walled cities (Jorvik, Lunden, Wincestre). Ubisoft said it would not be 'the largest or biggest game in the series' and would 'respect players' time' after Odyssey's bloat. No official km² figure was found.
findings.lesson: Two points line up with Kapman's plans. First, river stretches as their own hand-made places joined to the main map, like the GDD's true-width river places. Second, a few named towns for a whole kingdom, which supports cutting minor ports and towns on the more-shrunk comparison maps.

findings.name: Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag (the Caribbean)
findings.what: A large section of the Caribbean shrunk into a dense sea of small islands, sailed freely in the Jackdaw. Fast travel opens only after a place is discovered.
findings.numbers: About 50 locations (atolls, sea forts, Mayan ruins, plantations, wrecks). Main cities: Havana, Kingston, Nassau, plus Port-au-Prince and Inagua. Designed as roughly 60% land and 40% sea. Estimates (not published): sailing between major ports takes a few real minutes, and the length scale is somewhere around 1:100-1:300.
findings.lesson: Heavy shrinking plus densely packed islands means the sea is never empty and sailing was widely praised. The price is that a crossing never feels like a voyage. This is the opposite end of the range from Kapman, useful as the 'too short' benchmark on the comparison maps.

findings.name: Ghost of Tsushima (one real island, reshaped)
findings.what: The game keeps the real island's outline but invents the land inside. The developers said the team 'did not intend to create a one-to-one recreation'. There are no waypoints; a guiding wind shows the way.
findings.numbers: The real island is 696 km² and about 70 x 15 km. The developers say a faithful island would be 'endless forest and mountains', so they added open grassland to make more of it walkable. The wind feature took about 1 week to build and about 1 year to tune. The in-game scale is not published.
findings.lesson: Keep the outlines players will recognise (coasts, river mouths, headlands) and freely reshape what lies inside for play. A strong guiding feature that lives in the world itself (here the wind) made travel itself the experience. For a sailing game, the real wind and the stars are the natural equivalent.

findings.name: Sea of Thieves / Skull and Bones (what makes sea time fun or dull)
findings.what: Sea of Thieves: a fictional sea sailed by crews who split the jobs (helm, sails, navigation, cannons, crow's nest). Skull and Bones: the Indian Ocean, with a ship whose speed is limited by a stamina bar.
findings.numbers: Sea of Thieves' designer set the spacing so a player sees another player's ship every 15-30 minutes. Reviews were split on solo sailing ('boring', 'maddening' versus 'relaxing', 'entertaining'), and one critic wished 'more emergent events would happen in the ocean'. Estimate: crossing the whole map takes roughly 15-20 minutes. Skull and Bones reviews: 'too much of a grind for too little reward', 'Dead in the Water'.
findings.lesson: A crossing's length is not the problem; long stretches with nothing to do or see are. Plan an encounter, sighting or decision every 10-30 minutes, plus real work on board (sail trim, lookout, navigation, crew). Artificial speed limits (stamina) read as grind.

findings.name: Sid Meier's Pirates!, Uncharted Waters, Crusader Kings 3 (travel on a 2D chart)
findings.what: Long voyages feel long through days passing, supplies and events, not real minutes. Pirates!: most play time is sailing between Caribbean ports, and the westward trade winds change your speed. Uncharted Waters: real ports on a world chart, where days pass and food and water run down (general knowledge, unverified here). CK3: travel is drawn on the map and fires events by distance travelled.
findings.numbers: CK3: one random event for every 20 baronies travelled; speed bonuses such as +10 (hired guards) and +20 (make haste). Pirates! (2004): Metacritic 88 on PC, over 1.5 million sold. Uncharted Waters (1992) was criticised for 'flawed and repetitive' play and 'inaccurate geography'.
findings.lesson: For Kapman's 2D chart mode, compression can be extreme because travel is abstract there. Make legs feel long through days, supplies and crew mood, and trigger events by distance (like CK3's 20 baronies) rather than by time. Reviewers noticed when the geography was wrong, so keep the real outlines even on the chart.

findings.name: Microsoft Flight Simulator and Kingdom Come (true 1:1, the contrast)
findings.what: MSFS is the whole Earth at 1:1, streamed from Bing/Azure map data with AI-built 3D scenery. Kingdom Come: Deliverance is 1:1 in spirit but covers only the small Sázava-Rattay corner of Bohemia.
findings.numbers: MSFS: over 2 million cities and towns, 1.5 billion buildings, 2 trillion trees, 37,000 airports; Metacritic 91. It works because airliners fly at about 250 m/s, and long flights still take hours. A 2.25 m/s boat at 1:1 would need about 53 real hours from Dorestad to London (my calc: 430 km / 8.1 km/h).
findings.lesson: 1:1 only suits fast vehicles or small areas. For Kapman, true size belongs only to the boat's own surroundings: rivers, harbours, river mouths and towns, which is what the GDD already does.

findings.name: Synthesis: scale options for Kapman's comparison maps
findings.what: Each scale applied to Kapman's real numbers: boat at 2.25 m/s = 8.1 km/h, clock 60x, Dorestad to London about 430 km, Bergen to east Iceland about 1,100 km. All my calculations.
findings.numbers: Real km covered per real hour = 8.1 x the scale factor. Dorestad to London: 1:1 = 53 h; 1:20 = 2.7 h; 1:32 = 1.7 h; 1:40 = 1.3-1.6 h; 1:60 = 53 min (boat reads its true speed by the game clock, about 2.2 game days); 1:100 = 32 min (the GDD's 'about 30 min'). Bergen to Iceland: 1:40 = 3.4 h; 1:60 = 2.3 h; 1:100 = 1.4 h. For comparison, other games: Odyssey about 1:38 and The Crew about 1:45 with fast vehicles; ETS2 1:19 countryside with towns at about 1:3; Black Flag roughly 1:100-1:300 (estimate). Whole Kapman world at 1:40: about 370 x 220 km of game space, from the 1:32 figure of 460 x 275 km.
findings.lesson:
What tends to work for a sailing game:
(1) Uneven scale. Ports, river mouths and rivers at 1:1-1:3; coastal seas around 1:40-1:60; open ocean shrunk hardest (1:100 or more).
(2) A single leg of about 20-60 real minutes feels like a voyage. Multi-hour legs (Norway to Iceland, Greenland) need events or work every 10-30 minutes and saving at any time.
(3) Keep coastline outlines and landmarks recognisable, and drop minor ports and towns as the scale shrinks (Valhalla shows 3 cities for England).
(4) Matching the scale to the clock (1:60 with a 60x clock) keeps in-game days honest.
findings.source: Calculations from the figures above; scale decision notes in C:\Users\joeyw\.claude\projects\C--Users-joeyw\memory\kapman-scale-decision.md

findings.name: Honest-calendar check: 1:30 to 1:37 makes the game calendar match real voyages
findings.what: With the clock at 60x (1 s = 1 game minute) and the boat at its real speed, a voyage's game-calendar length is 60 x D / (k x v_boat). It equals the real historic duration when k = 60 x v_hist / v_boat, where v_hist is the average progress of a real voyage, waits included. Two dated 9th-century itineraries give that number. Wulfstan sailed from Hedeby to Truso in 'seven days and nights... under sail all the way'. Ohthere had 3 + 2 days from Sciringes heal (Kaupang) to Hedeby.
findings.numbers: Hedeby-Truso is 638 km straight (my great-circle calculation), about 700 km by sea (estimate). Over 168 h that is about 1.1 m/s, so honest k = 60 x 1.1 / 2.25, about 1:30. Check: at 1:30 the run is 23.3 km of game, 2.9 h real, 7.2 game days. Kaupang-Hedeby is 506 km straight, about 600 km by sea (estimate); over 5 days that is about 1.4 m/s, so honest k is about 1:37. At the current 1:40, Hedeby-Truso takes 118 min real, 4.9 game days, 2.1 days short of history. At 1:150 it takes 1.3 game days.
findings.lesson: The current 1:40 is already almost the scale that keeps the calendar honest with no date jumps. Every stronger compression of a sea needs a date jump at the join equal to (historic days - game days). That gives a rule for the 'date jumps at joins' decision: compress any sea as hard as you like and add the missing days at the join. Stated on each map as 'game days vs history days', it lets the user judge scale by both feel and the calendar.
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wulfstan_of_Hedeby ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohthere_of_H%C3%A5logaland ; distances: my haversine calculation (route lengths are estimates)

findings.name: A river kept at true width cannot be shortened along its length by more than about 2x
findings.what: Natural meanders scale with channel width. Meander wavelength is 10-14 channel widths (average 11), and the radius of curvature is 2-3 widths (Leopold and Wolman). If length is compressed by k but width is kept at 1:1, the wavelength falls to about 11/k widths. This holds for every technique below, so the river-width-vs-boat question is separate from the sea-scale question.
findings.numbers: At k=2 the wavelength is about 5.5 widths and the bend radius 1-1.5 widths: hairpins, the limit of believable. At k=40 it is 0.28 widths: bends overlap, physically impossible. A meandering river has sinuosity of 1.5-4 by definition, so straightening it gains only 1.5-4x and removes its character. Visual check: the Thames from its estuary to London is about 120 km real. At 1:40 that is 3 km of game, against a true width of roughly 250-300 m (estimate), so the river reads as a stubby 10:1 lake.
findings.lesson: On every scale map, draw rivers as 1:1 insets (the GDD's chain of river places with the dull reaches cut), not as compressed lines at true width. The sea and land scale can then be chosen freely, because the boat-to-river ratio only ever appears inside 1:1 places. The maps should show both: the compressed world with the river as a thin symbol line, and a zoomable 1:1 'bead' for each river place.

findings.name: Euro Truck Simulator 2 / American Truck Simulator: roads compressed, destinations not, scale changes kept bounded
findings.what: SCS builds Europe at 1:19 and the US at 1:20. The truck drives at real speed, and cities are shown as a few representative blocks at much lighter compression than the roads. The UK was built at 1:15, and SCS says a rework will bring it in line. The mismatch inside one continuous drivable world was treated as a flaw.
findings.numbers: ETS2 1:19 (UK 1:15); ATS 1:20 (Wikipedia). City compression is community-reported at about 1:3-1:5 (unverified this session). Comparison: 1,000 km real at 1:19 is 52.6 km, about 40 min at 80 km/h. The same 1,000 km at Kapman's 1:40 is 25 km, about 185 min at 2.25 m/s. Matching ETS2's trip times with a sailing boat about 10x slower than a truck would need about 1:190 at sea.
findings.lesson: Compress the connective tissue (open sea) the most and the destinations (ports, river places) the least, and change scale only at a join (river mouth, mist, headland), never in the middle of a sea. Pros: proven in a commercial real-speed driving game. Cons: a seam the player can sense if two regions they can sail between continuously have different scales. Kapman's 'levels that join' already fits this.

findings.name: Focus+context fisheye: home waters large, far lands compressed
findings.what: A radial warp around a focus. It uses the Sarkar-Brown graphical fisheye G(x) = (d+1)x/(dx+1), where x is real distance / R. Local magnification is d+1 at the centre and 1/(d+1) at the edge. The inverse is closed-form, x = y/(d+1-dy), so terrain can be baked by sampling the real DEM at inverse coordinates. Build effort: low for 2D (a per-vertex transform of the coastlines); medium for 3D.
findings.numbers: My calculation, focus 55N 5E, R=4,000 km, d=3, centre 1:40. The whole world fits a 50 km game disc (radius 25 km). Game distance from the centre: Hedeby 6.1 km, Dorestad 6.7, London 9.3, Kaupang 9.6, Reykjavik 19.2, Kiev 19.1, Brattahlid 23.0, Vinland 24.9 (at a uniform 1:40, Vinland would be 97.8 km). Local scale (radial/tangential): Dorestad 1:62/1:50, Reykjavik 1:221/1:94, Vinland 1:619/1:157. Legs at 2.25 m/s: Dorestad-London 51 min, Kaupang-Hedeby 68, Stad-East Horn 82, Reykjavik-Brattahlid 41, Brattahlid-Vinland 45, Bergen-Dublin 128 (it crosses the magnified middle).
findings.lesson: Pros: one continuous map; home waters feel big and the Atlantic is short. Cons: (1) far lands are flattened toward the focus by the radial/tangential ratio 3x+1, so Iceland is squashed about 2.4:1 and Vinland 3.9:1. No radial fisheye avoids this, because only the uniform map is conformal. (2) Travel time depends on where a leg sits relative to the focus, not only its length: Bergen-Dublin takes 3x as long as Brattahlid-Vinland. (3) The focus cannot move in a 3D world. Good as a 2D chart and as a comparison map; weak as the 3D world layout.
findings.source: Sarkar & Brown, 'Graphical Fisheye Views of Graphs', CHI '92 (formula from memory, not fetched this session); numbers are my own calculation

findings.name: Power-law leg times: uniform, square-root and metro-map are one dial
findings.what: Make each port-to-port leg take T = c x D^alpha minutes. alpha = 1 is a uniform scale. alpha = 0 is Harry Beck's Tube diagram: equal spacing, straight lines and 45-degree angles, central area enlarged; first published January 1933 in 700,000 copies, with a reprint a month later. alpha = 0.5, the square-root rule, sits between them: short hops stay near the current scale and ocean crossings shrink hard. Each leg gets its own scale, k = D / (v x T).
findings.numbers: Square-root rule anchored to the GDD's Dorestad-London 430 km = 30 min (c = 1.447 min per sqrt(km), v = 2.25 m/s), my calculation. 50 km hop: 10 min, local 1:36. 100 km: 14.5 min, 1:51. Dorestad-London: 30 min, 1:106. Kaupang-Hedeby: 32.5 min, 1:115. Hedeby-Truso: 36.5 min, 1:129. Novgorod-Kiev: 43 min, 1:154. Stad-East Horn: 46 min, 1:162. Brattahlid-Vinland: 51 min, 1:179. For comparison, at a uniform 1:40: 9 / 19 / 80 / 94 / 118 / 166 / 186 / 227 min. alpha = 0 would be, say, 12 min for every leg.
findings.lesson: Pros: one number (alpha) sets pacing, and the square-root rule keeps the current 1:40 feel near shore while cutting Atlantic legs to under an hour. Cons: it is a graph rule, not a map. Splitting a leg changes the total time (at alpha = 0.5, two halves take sqrt(2) x as long), so the leg list must be fixed. Pruning minor ports at small map scales must not change the in-game legs. Drawing it as a map needs a layout solver (next finding). Metro style (alpha = 0) loses the grandeur of ocean crossings.
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Beck ; leg numbers are my calculation from haversine distances

findings.name: Travel-time (time-space) cartograms: place ports by sailing time
findings.what: Distance cartograms move points so that map distance reflects travel time rather than kilometres, as in the London Underground travel-time cartogram centred on one station. The usual method: build an N x N travel-time matrix, place the ports by multidimensional scaling (classical MDS, or stress majorization for a better fit), then warp the coastlines with a thin-plate spline anchored on the ports. Spiekermann and Wegener's time-space maps showed Europe 'shrinking' with high-speed rail this way.
findings.numbers: For about 60 major ports the matrix is 60 x 60, which computes instantly; the work is in the data. Inputs could be the square-root rule above, or historic sailing days (Wulfstan 7 days, Ohthere 3+2 days; Landnamabok gives Stad to Horn in Iceland as 7 doegr, from memory and unverified, and a doegr may be 12 or 24 h). Build effort: medium, about a day for 2D. Baking 3D terrain through a spline warp is harder.
findings.lesson: Pros: the map is the true travel-time picture, and the 2D chart could show 'days at sea' directly. Cons: sailing times are asymmetric (the prevailing westerlies make a leg faster one way than the other) while MDS needs symmetric times, so average them. Conflicting times make coastlines bend or fold. Rivers are unaffected, because they stay 1:1 insets (finding 2).
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartogram (distance cartograms, London travel-time example); Spiekermann & Wegener 1994 'The shrinking continent', Environment and Planning B 21 (from memory, not fetched)

findings.name: Density-equalizing cartogram with content as the density (Gastner-Newman / flow-based)
findings.what: Gastner and Newman (PNAS 2004, vol. 101 no. 20) treat a variable as a density and diffuse it until it is equal everywhere, so each region's area becomes proportional to its value. The flow-based successor (Gastner, Seguy, More, PNAS 2018) 'takes only a few seconds even for complex and detailed input', where older methods took minutes. Open tools: go_cart in C (GeoJSON + a CSV of region id, value, name; no longer maintained) and the newer cartogram-cpp. For Kapman, the density would be content (ports + river places + events per cell), with a floor for open sea.
findings.numbers: Estimate. Suppose about 60% of the 240 approved ports sit in about 10% of the map area (North Sea, Danish waters, south Baltic), and the open ocean is about 50% of the area with a density floor of 10% of the mean. Then home waters grow about 2.4x in linear size and the ocean shrinks about 3.2x, a ratio of about 7-8 between them. With home waters at 1:40, the ocean would sit at roughly 1:300.
findings.lesson: Pros: content becomes evenly spaced, which is the 'no dull stretches' goal, and there is a ready tool. Cons: coastlines go blobby, and the sea-floor value is a design decision that sets how big the oceans feel. It is best as a 2D comparison map or as the target for zone scales, not as 3D terrain. The result depends on which ports are counted, so cutting minor ports changes the map.

findings.name: Portolan charts: true coasts, drawn hierarchy, built-in rules for cutting minor ports
findings.what: Medieval sea charts were drawn with ruler, dividers and coloured inks. The 32-direction colour-coded rhumb-line network came first, then coastlines copied from earlier charts, then names. Names are written perpendicular to the coast; red marks important ports and black marks minor places and hazards. Scale bars are in portolan miles. Coastlines were very realistic, but the charts ignored the Earth's curvature.
findings.numbers: 1 portolan mile (miglio) is about 1.25 km. Early charts measure about 69 x 49 cm (the Catalan Atlas of 1375 has 12 sheets and added the first illustrated compass rose). 32 rhumb directions.
findings.lesson: This gives the user's 'cut the less prominent towns' rule a period basis. Tier 1 in red, kept at every scale; tier 2 in black, dropped on small-scale sheets. Names stand perpendicular to the coast so a crowded coastline stays readable. A scale bar in both real km and game minutes ('1 hour of sailing') states each map's scale plainly. Style only; no build cost beyond drawing. It also suits the B&W look with warm red as the only accent.

findings.name: Tabula Peutingeriana and mappae mundi: importance over measure, distances written instead of drawn
findings.what: The Peutinger map is a Roman road itinerary copied around 1200: a single scroll on which land is stretched east-west, seas and rivers are squeezed into thin strips, and distances are written as numbers along each road rather than drawn to scale. Mappae mundi go further and draw by meaning: T-O layout, east at the top, Jerusalem in the centre.
findings.numbers: Peutinger: 6.75 m long x 0.35 m high (aspect about 19:1), 11 parchment sections, 555 cities and about 3,500 other place names. Hereford mappa mundi, about 1.5 m across (c. 1300); Ebstorf, 3.56 x 3.58 m; about 1,100 mappae mundi survive.
findings.lesson: The Peutinger form fits a long route very well. Laid out on one line, the whole road from Vinland to Kiev (about 8,000 km by sea and river, estimate) has no wasted ocean, and each sea is a narrow band labelled with its days. Pros: honest about being a schedule, easy to draw, and river places can hang off it as 1:1 beads. Cons: no geography for open-sea navigation. The mappa mundi is an art-direction reference (a world centred on your home port) more than a scale method.

findings.name: Pixel maths for high-resolution comparison maps where river widths are visible
findings.what: The user wants to zoom in and see river widths beside the boat. In the compressed world, true-width rivers and the 7.7 m boat are tiny in pixels, so whole-world sheets alone cannot show them. Each scale map needs a world sheet plus 1:1 insets, or a deep-zoom tiled image.
findings.numbers: Estimate: a uniform 1:40 world box of about 5,900 x 2,600 km real is about 147 x 65 km of game. At 16,384 px wide that is 9 m/px: the boat is 0.9 px and a 100 m river 11 px. At 65,536 px wide, 2.25 m/px: boat 3.4 px, 100 m river 44 px. A boat at least 15 px long needs 0.5 m/px, about 295,000 px wide (around 38 gigapixels), which is impractical. A 1:1 inset at 0.5 m/px is easy: a 2 km reach is 4,000 px. The fisheye world (50 km disc) at 16,384 px is about 3 m/px.
findings.lesson: Draw each candidate scale as one world sheet of 16-32k px, with tiered port labels, plus the same set of 1:1 river beads at 0.5 m/px (Dorestad, Traiectum, Lundenwic, Hedeby's Schlei, Novgorod, Kiev) with a boat silhouette and a 10 m bar. Use OpenSeadragon deep zoom if one zoomable page is wanted. River widths then compare the same way across every scale option.
findings.source: My calculation; boat 7.7 m and speed 2-2.5 m/s from the task brief

carto.summary:
Main result: the sea scale and the river scale are separate questions. Leopold and Wolman's meander ratios (wavelength about 11 channel widths) mean a river kept at true width cannot be compressed more than about 2x along its length, so rivers belong in 1:1 inset 'beads' (the GDD's chain of places) on every candidate map. The seas can take any of the variable-scale methods. Two dated voyages fix the current 1:40 against the calendar: Wulfstan (Hedeby-Truso, 7 days and nights) and Ohthere (Kaupang-Hedeby, 5 days). With the 60x clock they put the scale at which game days equal real days at about 1:30-1:37. Any harder sea compression just needs a date jump at the join (historic days minus game days). ETS2 (1:19, UK 1:15 being fixed, ATS 1:20) shows how this is usually done: compress the connecting routes, keep destinations, and change scale only at seams. All variable-scale options are one dial, leg time T = c x D^alpha: uniform (alpha=1), square-root (0.5), Beck metro (0). Fisheye, time-space MDS and density cartograms are ways to draw that dial as a continuous map, each with the shape costs given in the findings.

Three surprise maps worth drawing:

(1) Square-root sea-days portolan. Ports are placed by stress-majorization MDS so that each leg takes T = 1.447 x sqrt(km) minutes at 2.25 m/s (anchored to Dorestad-London 430 km = 30 min). Short hops come out at about 1:36, close to today's feel; the North Sea at about 1:106-1:130; the Atlantic legs at about 1:160-1:180. Leg times: Kaupang-Hedeby 32.5 min (4.4 km of game), Hedeby-Truso 36.5 min (4.9 km), Stad-East Horn 46 min (6.2 km), Brattahlid-Vinland 51 min (6.8 km). Draw it in portolan style: 32-wind rhumb lines from Hedeby, names perpendicular to the coast, about 40 tier-1 ports in red kept at all zooms, the rest in black and dropped on the small sheet. The scale bar reads in minutes and game days.

(2) North Sea fisheye. Focus 55N 5E, R = 4,000 km, Sarkar-Brown d = 3, so the scale is 1:40 at the centre and about 1:620 radially at the rim, and the whole world fits a 50 km game disc (16,384 px is about 3 m/px). Hedeby sits 6.1 km from the centre, Dorestad 6.7, London 9.3, Reykjavik 19.2, Kiev 19.1, Vinland 24.9. Overlay rings every 500 km real so the warp shows. Label the leg times: Dorestad-London 51 min, Stad-Horn 82, Brattahlid-Vinland 45. That makes its strength (big home waters) and its flaw (Iceland flattened about 2.4:1, time set by position rather than distance) plain to see.

(3) The Peutinger river road. One 19:1 scroll (for example 32,768 x 1,700 px) running Vinland - Greenland - Iceland - Norway - Hedeby - Birka - Neva - Ladoga - Volkhov - Novgorod - Dnieper - Kiev, about 8,000 km (estimate). Seas are narrow bands with history days and game minutes written on them, as the Romans wrote miles. Below the scroll hang 1:1 beads at 0.5 m/px (a 2 km reach is 4,000 px) for Dorestad, Lundenwic, the Schlei, Novgorod and Kiev, each with a 7.7 m boat silhouette (15 px), so true river width beside the boat can be judged directly.

Caveats: this session's web-search budget was used up, so sources came from direct page fetches. Sarkar-Brown, Spiekermann-Wegener, the Landnamabok sailing days and the ETS2 city scale are from memory and flagged unverified. All leg distances and scale figures are my own great-circle calculations, and sea-route lengths are estimates.
